newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin breaks off holiday, Kremlin blames weather.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin breaks off holiday, Kremlin blames weather.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin unexpectedly broke off his holiday and headed for Moscow on Wednesday, the Kremlin said, blaming bad weather at the Black Sea resort of Sochi.

Yeltsin, shown earlier on television discussing tensions in southern Russia near the breakaway Chechen republic with Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov, underwent heart surgery last November and only returned to work full time in February.
But presidential spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky ruled out any health reason for Yeltsin's return to Moscow on Wednesday evening from the southern Russian resort.
"His departure is linked to just one circumstance -- bad weather," Yastrzhembsky told a Russian reporter who asked if the move could be linked to illness.

Television pictures showed sunny weather in Sochi, which is in the region where two bomb attacks have killed at least four people over the past two weeks. Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had decided to return on Monday before the weather improved.
"The president stuck to his decision even though the weather in Sochi is improving a little," he said.
The president also met First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov to discuss next steps in the government's anti-corruption campaign and tighter state control over the alcohol market.
Nemtsov, appointed last month to a team of young reformers, faces the unenviable task of tackling powerful vested interests in the Russian economy which have starved the budget of cash.

Kulikov said after meeting Yeltsin that police were taking steps to reinforce security in southern Russia but were not planning to send any fresh troops. "There are no plans to build up troops in the area," he told Russian Public Television.
The situation around Chechnya, where 21 months of war between Moscow troops and rebels ended in a shaky truce in August, has deteriorated badly in the past week.
Bombs in two towns, each a few hundred km (miles) from Sochi, have killed at least four people and injured dozens.

"We have taken certain measures to prevent the infiltration of criminals from Chechnya," Kulikov said. "But this does not mean at all sealing off the border between Russia and Chechnya." "What we want is a full control over it," he added.
Chechen separatist leaders have denied any part in the attacks which they said were "dirty tricks" by Russia. They called on Kulikov to either prove or retract his allegations.
Negotiators on both sides said they were committed to peace despite the tensions, aggravated on Wednesday by the murder of a senior local official.
Yeltsin's senior aides, Boris Berezovsky and Ivan Rybkin, rushed to the Chechen capital Grozny to meet the separatists to try to keep up the political dialogue.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted Rybkin as saying forces on both sides wanted to fuel hostility around Chechnya.
"Many people in Chechnya and in Russia want to disrupt the fragile peace, but we shall block such attempts," Rybkin said without specifying who exactly he meant.

Yeltsin wore a sweater for his meeting with Kulikov although the temperature, according to a meteorological official, was around 18 degrees Celsius (64 Fahrenheit). She said there could be cloud and it had been raining there over the past few days.

A Kremlin spokesman in Moscow said Yeltsin would return to his Gorky-9 residence, west of the capital on Wednesday evening. He had recorded a radio address to the nation to be broadcast on Thursday, when Russians celebrate Labour Day and the arrival of spring, and opposition communists are expected to hold big rallies in Moscow.

Yeltsin has had a busy schedule since he returned to the Kremlin in February. Next week he is due to meet Spanish King Juan Carlos and on May 27 he expects to travel to Paris where he has said he wants to sign a partnership deal with NATO.

Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said on Wednesday Moscow was still aiming for a May 27 deal but again urged the alliance, which plans to invite in some of Moscow's former allies in July, not to move its military might into new member states.
